batch_notes: Both targets have every bug record already attributed directly to a Hegel property, so no attributions were needed. Shape worth noting: in go/apd, 17 of 34 properties are per-bug narrowed properties (comments start with 'apd/N:', names describe the correct behaviour, inputs are constrained to the failing region) and the README itself calls them 'pinned'; I tagged all of them pin. Each bug's bugs_direct points at its own narrowed property, so a naive direct-attribution count would say 17 general properties found nothing and 17 pins found one each, whereas the README makes clear the broad Python-oracle properties are what surfaced most divergences (they now Assume/skip around the pinned cases, e.g. apd/2 and apd/3 in TestHegelSetStringAgreesWithPythonDecimal). In go/bbolt the README states both bugs 'came from reading Bucket.MoveBucket and were confirmed with a probe before the properties were written', so the two pin-tagged properties reproduce rather than discovered the bugs; the direct attribution should be read with that in mind. Rubric gaps: (1) 'a valid computation must raise a documented condition flag / error on overflow' (apd/7) sits between rejection and spec-postcondition; (2) 'helpers' bundle properties (TestHegelDecimalHelpersAgreeWithTheModel, TestHegelConversionsAgreeWithStrconv, TestHegelTextFormatsAgreeWithTheModel) mix model, round trip and postcondition checks and the category depends heavily on which check is read as leading; (3) aliasing independence (result pointer == operand pointer) is a recurring Go shape that fits internal-consistency only loosely. The Python decimal child-process oracle and the model-of-a-B+tree driver are both conventional in design and were not tagged interesting at the property level.
